stem:
Tejas cuts paper strips of $9\,\mathrm{cm}$ and $12\,\mathrm{cm}$ to make matching-length torans. He wants the shortest common length both strip sizes can make.

Which claim is correct?

options.text: Any common multiple of $9$ and $12$ is the shortest common length.
The shortest common length is $9\times 12=108\,\mathrm{cm}$, with no smaller shared multiple.
The shortest common length is the LCM of $9$ and $12$, which is $36\,\mathrm{cm}$.
The shortest common length is $9+12=21\,\mathrm{cm}$ because those are the printed strip lengths.

teacher.key_rationale: The earliest common reach of repeating $9$ cm and $12$ cm lengths is their LCM. $\mathrm{LCM}(9,12)=36$. Any common multiple is not automatically the shortest; the product $108$ is a common multiple but not the least; adding the printed lengths is not the LCM rule.
